paragraphs.heading: A shell in pieces
paragraphs.text: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's lithosphere is made up of a number of large tectonic plates that have been moving slowly since 3–4 billion years ago. The lithosphere is the planet's rigid outer shell, and it includes the crust and the upper mantle. Depending on how they are defined, there are seven or eight major plates, and many minor ones besides. The theory builds on continental drift, an idea worked out in the first decades of the 20th century. Geoscientists came to accept plate tectonics once the spreading of the seafloor had been validated, in the mid- to late 1960s.

paragraphs.heading: Rigid plates on a softer layer
paragraphs.text: Earth's outer layers are divided into the lithosphere and, beneath it, the asthenosphere. The lithosphere is the cooler and more rigid of the two, and the asthenosphere is hotter and flows more easily. The plates are relatively rigid and float across this ductile layer below them. The key principle of the theory is that the lithosphere exists as separate, distinct plates riding on the asthenosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates meet
paragraphs.text: The place where two plates meet is called a plate boundary. The way the plates move relative to each other sets the type of boundary, which can be convergent, divergent or transform. Boundaries are where geological events happen, such as earthquakes and the making of mountains, volcanoes, mid-ocean ridges and oceanic trenches. The vast majority of the world's active volcanoes lie along plate boundaries. The Pacific plate's Ring of Fire is the most active and the most widely known.

paragraphs.heading: The conveyor belt
paragraphs.text: Along convergent boundaries, a process called subduction takes the edge of one plate down beneath the other and into the mantle. This shrinks Earth's total surface area. The loss is made up along divergent margins, where seafloor spreading forms new oceanic crust. The two processes together keep the total surface area constant, like a tectonic conveyor belt.

paragraphs.heading: What moves the plates
paragraphs.text: Density differences from place to place in the mantle set up convection currents, a slow creeping motion of Earth's solid mantle. Plates move away from a seafloor spreading ridge, which is a high point in the terrain. The newly formed crust cools as it travels, grows denser, and so adds to the motion. At a subduction zone, relatively cold and dense oceanic crust sinks into the mantle, and this is the strongest driver of plate motion. How much other proposed factors matter, such as tidal drag from the Moon, is still debated.

paragraphs.heading: As slow as fingernails
paragraphs.text: Relative to one another, plates typically move at anywhere from zero to 10 cm a year. At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the motion is 10 to 40 millimetres per year, about the speed at which fingernails grow. The Nazca plate moves at about 160 millimetres per year, about the speed at which hair grows.

paragraphs.heading: Ocean floor and continents
paragraphs.text: Plates are topped by one or two types of crust, oceanic and continental. Oceanic crust is formed at sea-floor spreading centers. It is denser than continental crust, since it holds less silicon and more of the heavier elements. Because of that difference in density, oceanic crust generally sits below sea level, and continental crust rises buoyantly above it.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond Earth
paragraphs.text: Earth is the only planet known to have active plate tectonics at present. Even so, evidence suggests that other planets and moons have had, or still show, forms of tectonic activity. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, shows signs of plates of icy crust that move and interact, much as Earth's plates do. Mars and Venus are thought to have been tectonically active in the past, though not in the same form as Earth.
